ja: 一段・五段・する・来る
kana: いちだん・ごだん・する・くる
name: verb groups
english: Every verb is in one of three groups, and the group decides how it changes.
use: Check a new verb's group once; every form follows from it.
formation: Ichidan verbs end in -iru or -eru and just drop ru (taberu → tabe-). Godan verbs change their last syllable (kau → kawanai, kaimasu). Only suru and kuru are irregular.

example.ja: ご飯食べて、すぐ帰ったよ。
example.english: I ate and went straight home.

examplePolite.ja: ご飯を食べて、すぐ帰りました。
examplePolite.english: I ate and went straight home.

notes: Lookalikes: kaeru (go home), hairu, shiru, hashiru, iru (need) and kiru (cut) end in -iru/-eru but are godan: kaetta, haitta, shitte. Kiru (wear) and iru (be) are ichidan.

ja: 書か・書き・書け・書こ
kana: かか・かき・かけ・かこ
name: the four stems
english: Godan verbs shift their last vowel to a, i, e or o to fit the ending.
use: Know which ending takes which vowel and you can build most forms of any godan verb.
formation: Godan: a before -nai (kakanai), i before -masu and -tai (kakimasu), e before -ba and can-do (kakeba, kakeru), o plus u for let's (kakou). Ichidan just drops ru and adds the ending (tabenai, tabemasu). Watch the sounds: a final u becomes wa (kawanai), tsu becomes chi (machimasu), su becomes shi (hanashimasu).

example.romaji: ima wa kawanai kedo, raigetsu kaou kana
example.ja: 今は買わないけど、来月買おうかな。
example.english: I'm not buying it now, but maybe next month.

examplePolite.romaji: ima wa kaimasen ga, raigetsu kaou to omoimasu
examplePolite.ja: 今は買いませんが、来月買おうと思います。
examplePolite.english: I won't buy it now, but I think I'll buy it next month.

notes: Verbs ending in a vowel plus u take wa before -nai: kau → kawanai, iu → iwanai (not kaanai).

name: te/ta sound changes
english: Godan verbs change sound before -te and -ta, depending on their last syllable.
use: -te, -ta, -tara and -teru all share these changes, so drilling them once pays off everywhere.
formation: Ichidan: drop ru, add te (tabete). Godan: u/tsu/ru → tte, mu/bu/nu → nde, ku → ite, gu → ide, su → shite. Exceptions: iku → itte, suru → shite, kuru → kite; -ta works the same way.

example.romaji: eki made aruite, densha ni notta
example.ja: 駅まで歩いて、電車に乗った。
example.english: I walked to the station and got on the train.

examplePolite.romaji: eki made aruite, densha ni norimashita
examplePolite.ja: 駅まで歩いて、電車に乗りました。
examplePolite.english: I walked to the station and got on the train.

notes: iku → itte, not iite. Some forms sound the same: itte can come from iku (go) or iu (say), katte from kau (buy) or katsu (win).

ja: する・来る・行く・ある・いい
kana: する・くる・いく・ある・いい
name: the exceptions
english: The few verbs (plus the adjective ii) that break the patterns.
use: They are among the most common words in speech, so their odd forms come up constantly.
formation: suru → shinai, shite, dekiru (can); kuru → konai, kite, korareru (can). iku → itte, itta; aru → nai; ii → yokunai, yokatta. Honorifics irassharu, kudasaru, ossharu and nasaru take -aimasu: irasshaimasu, kudasaimasu.

example.romaji: jikan nai kara, kyou wa konai tte
example.ja: 時間ないから、今日は来ないって。
example.english: He says he has no time, so he's not coming today.

examplePolite.romaji: jikan ga nai node, kyou wa konai sou desu
examplePolite.ja: 時間がないので、今日は来ないそうです。
examplePolite.english: Apparently he has no time, so he isn't coming today.

notes: There is no aranai or kunai: aru → nai, kuru → konai.

name: dictionary form
english: Plain present and future: I do, I will do.
use: The everyday verb form with friends and family. It also goes before a noun to describe it: taberu mono (things to eat).
formation: It's the form you find in the dictionary, so nothing changes. Every verb ends in u: ichidan in -iru/-eru, godan in u, ku, gu, su, tsu, nu, bu, mu or ru; plus suru and kuru.

example.ja: 明日何時に来る？
example.english: What time are you coming tomorrow?

examplePolite.romaji: ashita nan ji ni kimasu ka?
examplePolite.english: What time are you coming tomorrow?

notes: There's no separate future tense: taberu covers both 'I eat' and 'I'll eat'. For 'I'm eating now', use -te iru.

name: polite present
english: Polite present and future: I do, I will do.
use: With strangers, staff, colleagues and anyone you'd call -san. The safe default while you're learning.
formation: Ichidan: drop ru, add masu (tabemasu). Godan: change the last u to i, add masu (kaimasu, machimasu, hanashimasu). suru → shimasu, kuru → kimasu.

example.romaji: kono densha wa shibuya ni ikimasu ka?
example.ja: この電車は渋谷に行きますか？
example.english: Does this train go to Shibuya?

notes: The final u is nearly silent: tabemasu sounds like 'tabemas'.

name: plain negative
english: Plain negative: I don't, I won't.
use: The everyday 'don't / won't' with friends and family. -nai desu is a softer polite option.
formation: Ichidan: drop ru, add nai (tabenai). Godan: change the last u to a, add nai (kakanai, matanai); a final u becomes wa (kawanai). suru → shinai, kuru → konai, aru → nai.

example.ja: 今日は行かない。ちょっと疲れた。
example.english: I'm not going today. I'm a bit tired.

examplePolite.ja: 今日は行きません。ちょっと疲れました。
examplePolite.english: I'm not going today. I'm a bit tired.

notes: With a rising tone, ikanai? is an invitation (want to go?), not just a question.

name: polite negative
english: Polite negative: I don't, I won't.
use: Politely saying you don't or won't do something, including polite refusals.
formation: Swap -masu for -masen: tabemasen, kaimasen, machimasen. suru → shimasen, kuru → kimasen.

example.ja: すみません、お酒は飲みません。
example.english: Sorry, I don't drink alcohol.

notes: In everyday polite talk -nai desu (tabenai desu) is also common and sounds a little softer.

name: plain past
english: Plain past: I did.
use: Casually telling what happened; with mou it means 'already' (mou tabeta).
formation: Same sound changes as -te, with a instead of e: tabeta, katta, nonda, kaita, oyoida, hanashita. iku → itta, suru → shita, kuru → kita.

example.ja: 昨日、あの映画見た？
example.english: Did you see that movie yesterday?

examplePolite.romaji: kinou, ano eiga o mimashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 昨日、あの映画を見ましたか？
examplePolite.english: Did you see that movie yesterday?

notes: -ta also marks a discovery right now: a, atta! means 'oh, here it is!', not 'it was here'.

name: polite past
english: Polite past: I did.
use: Telling what happened to people you speak politely to. Set phrases too: wakarimashita (understood), arigatou gozaimashita.
formation: Swap -masu for -mashita: tabemashita, kaimashita, ikimashita. suru → shimashita, kuru → kimashita.

example.romaji: shuumatsu wa tomodachi to umi ni ikimashita
example.ja: 週末は友達と海に行きました。
example.english: I went to the beach with friends at the weekend.

notes: The i is nearly silent: tabemashita sounds like 'tabemashta'.

name: plain negative past
english: Plain negative past: I didn't.
use: Casually saying something didn't happen.
formation: Make the -nai form, then swap nai for nakatta: tabenakatta, kawanakatta, ikanakatta. suru → shinakatta, kuru → konakatta.

example.ja: 今朝は何も食べなかった。
example.english: I didn't eat anything this morning.

examplePolite.romaji: kesa wa nani mo tabemasen deshita
examplePolite.ja: 今朝は何も食べませんでした。
examplePolite.english: I didn't eat anything this morning.

notes: For 'haven't done it yet', use mada -tenai (mada tabetenai), not mada tabenakatta.

name: polite negative past
english: Polite negative past: I didn't.
use: Politely saying something didn't happen, often in apologies: shirimasen deshita (I didn't know).
formation: Take -masen and add deshita: tabemasen deshita, kaimasen deshita. suru → shimasen deshita, kuru → kimasen deshita.

example.ja: すみません、全然気づきませんでした。
example.english: Sorry, I didn't notice at all.

notes: In conversation -nakatta desu (tabenakatta desu) is just as common and a little softer.

name: te-form
english: Links actions (and then), gives a reason, or on its own asks someone to do something.
use: Everywhere: chaining what you did, explaining why, and casual requests like chotto matte.
formation: Ichidan: drop ru, add te (tabete). Godan: u/tsu/ru → tte, mu/bu/nu → nde, ku → ite, gu → ide, su → shite. iku → itte, suru → shite, kuru → kite.

example.ja: ちょっと待って、すぐ行くから。
example.english: Hang on, I'll be right there.

examplePolite.ja: ちょっと待ってください、すぐ行きます。
examplePolite.english: Just a moment, please. I'll be right there.

notes: The tense comes from the last verb: okite, gohan tabete, dekaketa = I got up, ate and left.

name: polite request
english: Please do...
use: Asking politely, for example to staff or strangers, and in instructions.
formation: te-form plus kudasai: tabete kudasai, matte kudasai, nonde kudasai. suru → shite kudasai, kuru → kite kudasai.

example.ja: すみません、もう一度言ってください。
example.english: Sorry, please say that again.

notes: kudasai still sounds like an instruction; to ask a favour, -te kuremasen ka or -te moraemasen ka is softer.

name: please don't
english: Don't...; also 'without doing'.
use: Asking someone not to do something: -naide with friends, -naide kudasai politely. Also 'without': nani mo tabenaide deta (left without eating).
formation: Make the -nai form and add de: tabenaide, kawanaide, ikanaide. suru → shinaide, kuru → konaide. Add kudasai to make it polite.

example.ja: 心配しないで。大丈夫だから。
example.english: Don't worry. I'm fine.

examplePolite.romaji: shinpai shinaide kudasai. daijoubu desu kara
examplePolite.ja: 心配しないでください。大丈夫ですから。

notes: 'Please don't' is -naide, not -nakute: tabenaide (don't eat it).

name: ongoing or state
english: Is doing, or is in a state (is married, knows, lives somewhere).
use: What someone is doing right now, ongoing habits, and states like shitteru (know) and kekkon shiteru (married). -teru is how it sounds in speech.
formation: te-form plus iru; in speech the i drops: tabeteru, matteru, nonderu. suru → shiteru, kuru → kiteru.

example.ja: ねえ、今何してるの？
example.english: Hey, what are you doing right now?

examplePolite.romaji: ima nani o shite imasu ka?
examplePolite.english: What are you doing right now?

notes: With change verbs it's the result, not the action: kekkon shiteru = is married, kiteru = has come (is here).

name: was doing
english: Was doing, or had been in a state.
use: Setting the scene in a story (what you were doing when...), and past states like 'I used to live in...'.
formation: te-form plus ita; in speech the i drops: tabeteta, matteta, nondeta. suru → shiteta, kuru → kiteta.

example.ja: ごめん、さっきまでずっと寝てた。
example.english: Sorry, I was asleep until just now.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, sakki made zutto nete imashita
examplePolite.ja: すみません、さっきまでずっと寝ていました。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I was asleep until just now.

notes: shitteta means 'I knew'; 'I didn't know' is shiranakatta, not shittenakatta.

name: not doing, not yet
english: Isn't doing; or hasn't done (yet).
use: With mada, it's how you say you haven't done something yet.
formation: te-form plus inai; in speech the i drops: tabetenai, mattenai, nondenai. suru → shitenai, kuru → kitenai.

example.romaji: mada hirugohan tabetenai n da yo
example.ja: まだ昼ご飯食べてないんだよ。
example.english: I haven't had lunch yet.

examplePolite.ja: まだ昼ご飯を食べていません。

notes: 'Not yet' is mada -tenai, not -nakatta. And 'I don't know' is shiranai, not shittenai.

name: want to
english: Want to do.
use: Saying what you want to do, or asking a friend what they want to do.
formation: Take the -masu stem and add tai: tabetai, kaitai, machitai, nomitai. suru → shitai, kuru → kitai. It then bends like an i-adjective: -takunai (don't want to), -takatta (wanted to).

example.ja: なんか甘いもの食べたいな。
example.english: I kind of want something sweet.

examplePolite.romaji: nanika amai mono ga tabetai desu
examplePolite.ja: 何か甘いものが食べたいです。

notes: Use it for yourself or to ask the listener; for someone else, say -tagatteru (kodomo ga asobitagatteru).

name: let's (casual)
english: Let's...; with to omou, I think I'll...
use: Casual suggestions to friends (ikou!), and plans: -ou to omotteru (I'm thinking of...).
formation: Ichidan: drop ru, add you (tabeyou, miyou). Godan: change the last u to o and add u (kaou, matou, nomou, ikou). suru → shiyou, kuru → koyou.

example.romaji: mou osoi shi, sorosoro kaerou ka
example.ja: もう遅いし、そろそろ帰ろうか。
example.english: It's late. Shall we head home?

examplePolite.romaji: mou osoi node, sorosoro kaerimashou ka
examplePolite.ja: もう遅いので、そろそろ帰りましょうか。
examplePolite.english: It's getting late. Shall we head home?

notes: Hold the long vowel: kaerou (let's go home) vs kaeru (go home).
